title: The Pump That Never Stops
principle: Blood goes round in a loop.

t: Your heart has beaten every few seconds since before you were born. It has never once had a rest.
Your heart started beating about three weeks after you were conceived and has not paused since. It will do roughly three billion beats without maintenance.
sub: Why does anything need pumping at all?
Before asking how it works, ask why the job exists.

question: Why does blood need pushing round instead of just sitting there?
Why is circulation necessary rather than simple diffusion through the body?
options: Because things spread far too slowly on their own
Because blood is heavy and would sink
Because the body would get cold
stages.outcome: Because things spread far too slowly on their own
note: Guess first — think about how long diffusion took in the membrane.
Commit. Diffusion time scales with the square of distance, which is the number that decides this.

t: Put each part of the loop in the right place.
Assemble the circuit: each component in the job it does.

label: Carries it away at high pressure
Carries blood away from the heart
Brings it back to the pump
Returns blood to the heart

t: Any part goes in any slot, so the marking is on you. Then it gets tested.
Placement is unconstrained. Assign each component, then the circuit is stress-tested — and every misassignment fails a different way.

label: Carries blood away under high pressure
Thin enough for exchange to happen

name: Move blood at all
Generate flow
pass: Blood leaves the heart under pressure.
Pressure is generated and conducted away from the pump.
fail: Nothing is pushing, or nothing is carrying it away.
No pressure source or no conducting vessel: there is no flow to speak of.

name: Actually deliver anything
Exchange
pass: Thin enough walls for oxygen to cross into tissue.
fail: Blood went round and never gave anything up.
Flow without a thin-walled exchange bed delivers nothing. Transport is not the purpose; exchange is.

name: Complete the circuit
Return
pass: It comes back, so it can go round again.
Venous return closes the loop and the circuit is continuous.
fail: Blood arrived somewhere and stayed there.
No return path: this is an open system, and it drains rather than circulates.

name: Work while standing up
Directionality against gravity
pass: It cannot run backwards down your legs.
One-way valves prevent retrograde flow in low-pressure vessels.
fail: It circulated beautifully lying down and pooled in your feet.
Venous pressure is too low to oppose gravity unaided — without valves, blood pools in the legs. This is exactly what varicose veins are.

win: A loop that works standing up. That is a circulation.
A complete closed circuit with directionality. Every part failed a different test, which is what tells you each is doing a distinct job.
lose: Read which test failed — it names what was in the wrong place.
Each failed trial names the function that was missing. Reassign and re-test.

t: Blood goes round in a loop. It never stops and never runs out.
This is a closed circulation: the same blood goes round and round, and the pump only has to keep it moving.
A closed double circulation — one circuit to the lungs, one to the body — driven by a four-chambered pump. Delivery happens only in the capillaries; everything else is plumbing.

Harvey worked out in 1628 that the blood must circulate, and he did it by arithmetic rather than dissection: the heart pumps more than the body's weight in blood every hour, so it cannot possibly be manufacturing it. It has to be the same blood coming back.
sub: The tiny pipes are where the useful bit happens.
Capillaries are where the whole system earns its keep; no cell in you is more than about two cells away from one.
The double circuit matters: it lets lung pressure stay low enough not to force fluid into the airways while body pressure stays high enough to reach your feet.

That separation of pressures is the reason a four-chambered heart appears independently in birds and mammals. A single circuit cannot satisfy both constraints at once, and the fix is the same fix twice.

q: Why can your body not just let things spread on their own?
Why is diffusion insufficient for a body your size?
Why does body size force the evolution of circulation?
options: Diffusion is fine over tiny distances and hopeless over big ones
Diffusion stops working once you are born
why: Diffusion is quick across a cell and impossibly slow across a body. Over a centimetre it would take hours, and you would be dead long before the oxygen arrived.

Diffusion time rises with the square of distance. Crossing a cell takes under a millisecond; crossing a centimetre of tissue would take hours. Circulation exists to carry things the long way quickly, so diffusion only ever has to cover the last few micrometres.

The t ∝ x² scaling is the whole argument, and it is why every animal above a millimetre or so has some form of bulk transport. It also explains capillary density: the system's job is to get a vessel within diffusion distance of every cell, which is why no cell in you sits more than about 20 micrometres from one.

t: A heart attack is a blocked pipe in the heart's own supply.

The heart cannot use the blood inside its chambers; it has its own small arteries on the outside. Block one and the muscle downstream dies within minutes — which is why a heart attack is a plumbing failure rather than a pump failure, and why unblocking the pipe quickly is the whole of the treatment.
